sourceInformation.plan: PLAN.md (claude-opus-5-5, max effort), scoped down by the builder where it disagreed with the time budget
sourceInformation.genre: On-rails light-gun shooter with a cover system
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge handoff v0.85.2 full engine (patched: PlayStation glyph default, mouse-wheel codes, audio bus), a custom painter's-order perspective renderer module ("Rail3D"), AI Hub session client 1.4.0 (protocol v1). No other libraries.
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native PS1-era pixel style: banded, fogged, flat-shaded perspective boxes with line textures, and the engine's Humanoid rigs as billboards
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural Humanoid rigs (crouch, point/aim, run, air, land, roll, climb, slash, die) driven by enemy state, plus code-posed boss machines (Stingray, Bulldog, Scylla, Seawolf)
sourceInformation.audio: All code: the engine chip synth and tracker for music and SFX, plus a Web Audio formant "Animalese" gibberish voice synth for every speaker
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, shared-world co-op for 1–4 players (host-authoritative Sim, input and snapshot messages); local two-player split screen
sourceInformation.testing: One command (node tests/run.mjs --all) prints only failures and a count: 824 checks over headless Node suites (game.advance, game.debug, direct Sim stepping), Autopilot playthroughs of every stage and of the whole ARCADE to the credits, the Training range, a Playwright browser smoke test, and the four AI Hub harness scenarios
sourceInformation.research: The engine handoff docs, the AI Hub protocol docs, and the Wikipedia article on Time Crisis 3 (summarised in PLAN.md). Facts used: pedal-based cover, 4 weapons, crisis flash, time limit per area, link play. Unknown: exact arcade time and weapon-switch rules.
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown
sourceInformation.perspective: First-person rail camera (cutscenes use a letterboxed rail shot)

testingFeedback: About 16 real defects were caught by scripted runs and validators (most before any screenshot): enemies shootable only through scenery (gallery floor, ice table, houses, deck crates), a boss whose defeat was never wired, a boss scene that never cleared, a lift whose cover prop stayed on the ground, a moving scene that let the camera pass living enemies, an endless cutscene loop after results, drones too fast to hit, and a Hammerhead fight that was unwinnable without shotgun shells.

7 of them were game-breaking soft-locks (a scene or boss that could never be finished): unreachable enemies, boss never defeated, boss scene never cleared, passing enemies in moving scenes, the lift with no cover, the endless cutscene loop, and Hammerhead with no ammo supply.

The most helpful tests were the scripted Autopilot playthrough of every stage (it finds soft-locks no assertion would) and the content validator that ray-casts every cover point from every player slot.

The least helpful were the screenshot checks for layout (slow for what they found) and the determinism hash test, which never failed; the net suite is covered by the real AI Hub harness instead of a fake hub.
engineFeedback: The fixed-step headless loop (game.advance, game.debug) that made every system testable in Node, plus the Humanoid rigs that draw from any View, and the ready-made pause menu, settings, rebinding and boot screen.

Yes: I assumed boot steps ran synchronously in Node (they need a tick), assumed the pixel font had a dash and the PlayStation face-button glyphs (it did not), and expected r.overlay in a split screen to give viewport-relative coordinates (it gives the whole buffer).
The perspective renderer ("Rail3D": camera math, painter-order boxes, sky, sea, fog, banded light), the deterministic Sim (cover, threats, director, bosses), the Autopilot, and the AI Hub netcode.
The 2D engine has no perspective view: rigs only draw from orthographic Views, so every enemy is drawn to a scratch canvas per frame, scaled by distance and sorted by hand, with no z-buffer.

Four small patches (engine/PATCHES.md): PlayStation glyphs by default (Xbox as the option), mouse-wheel input codes, audio.bus() for the voice synth, and extra pixel-font glyphs (face buttons, dashes, ellipsis, check, arrows).
A first-class first-person/rail view: a perspective E.View with depth-sorted rigs, boxes and sprites, so light-gun and corridor games do not need their own renderer.
promptFeedback: The plan's concrete numbers (timings, weapon tables, enemy roster, test suites) and the single-file, AI Hub and attract-mode requirements: they made every system verifiable.

The plan and TASK.md name different files and models, and the plan assumes the 3D engine and a very large scope (three stages, three bosses, online, split screen) that does not fit one medium-effort session without cuts.
Shipping everything at once: a feature-complete three-stage game with bosses, split screen, online co-op, a dev panel, an attract mode, and all audio and voices in code.
Add must/should/could tiers and say which plan items may be simplified, and supply the engine's perspective renderer or say plainly that none exists.

aiHub.name: Tide Crisis 3
aiHub.tagline: Duck. Pop. Shoot. Beat the tide.
aiHub.description: An original arcade light-gun rail shooter in PS1-style pixel 3D: duck behind cover, switch between four weapons and race each area's clock to retake an island's tidal barrier before the dawn king tide. Play solo, couch co-op or AI Hub co-op for up to four.
aiHub.controls: Mouse or stick aims · left click/R2 fires · hold right click/L2 for cover and reload · wheel/R1 switches weapons
